analysis.title: Macro Roadmap: Risk Jitters
key_insights: Central banks are uniform in prioritizing not adding to volatility. The Fed and ECB were both measured this week and weighted tighter financial conditions as a reason for caution, a shift from six weeks ago when the October ECB meeting priced 18bp of hikes and the Fed's October meeting priced 17bp at the end of September.

Inflation inputs lean hawkish: Brent is $9/bbl higher and TTF EUR16/MWh higher since mid-September, the market prices 4.5% Euro area headline inflation by Q1 next year, and the September US core inflation print was unambiguously strong. Offsetting this, Nasdaq 100 is nearly 9% off its early October high, US HY CDX is 20bp wider and OAT/Bund is about 60bp wider.

Financial conditions have tightened only modestly this year: about 35bp in the US (driven by long end rates and the dollar) and broadly flat in Europe, where a weaker euro offset tightening from rates, sovereign spreads and equities. Equities and credit are still a net easing for US financial conditions YTD. The concern is the direction of the tail if equity and credit moves gain steam.

GS sees the Fed and ECB on a quarterly hiking path after not hiking this week. December remains live and the pause buys time to assess the risk backdrop. Gradualism means slower and less proactive, but does not mean central banks will not hike if needed.

Rates are driven by AI capex (Nasdaq) and energy prices. Earlier in the year both pushed rates higher together. Now they conflict: energy keeps rising while AI spending sustainability is questioned. In October the correlation of daily 10y UST moves with NDX flipped to +0.60 and with Brent to -0.28, so 10y USTs rallied this month despite oil.

European rates are stuck between the two drivers. October correlations of 10y EUR swaps to NDX, Brent and TTF are all close to zero, and 1m realised vol on 10y EUR swaps is only 57bp annualised, yet implied vol trades at a premium because the equilibrium is not stable.
Scrutiny of the AI investment cycle is rising: the market asks who earns the returns and how the cycle is financed, with cash flow under pressure and financing needs rising.

GS scenarios for rates: de-escalation plus continued equity cracks drives a sustained rally in rates. Equities rebounding on AI resilience with energy still elevated drives the next leg higher in yields.

European natgas (TTF) broke through EUR100/MWh this week, 36% above the September close, on headlines of a post-midterm Middle East re-escalation. Hormuz LNG exports have dipped back to 20-25% of pre-war levels against the 65% by January that GIR's base case needs. NW European storage is 64% full, the lowest in 14 years, against a pre-2022 average of 88%.

GIR's TTF risk matrix: Hormuz recovery base case is 70; low Hormuz flows with normal weather need about 105 to force LNG demand destruction; cold winter with subdued Strait flows takes TTF to about 150. Mar27 at about 98 prices a high probability of the low-supply winter, so there is less asymmetry for longs than a month ago when TTF sat at 72, but the payoff remains convex in the severe scenario.

UK Budget was low-volatility and modest. Headroom against the deficit rule fell to GBP15bn from GBP24bn, in line with consensus. Major decisions (departmental cuts, health funding, defence to 3% of GDP by 2030) were deferred to next year's Spending Review, possibly as late as autumn, taking fiscal risk out of focus. Some further term premium reduction in gilts is possible.

BoE next week: a hike is nearly fully priced (24bp). GS base case is the MPC follows the quarterly gradualism of the Fed and ECB. December prices a 40% chance of a hike, so a clear quarterly signal would take premium out of the UK front end.

risk_factors: Equity and credit declines gaining steam could produce a severe tightening in financial conditions if growth has peaked.
AI capex sustainability and financing: cash flow under pressure and rising financing needs.
Energy supply: low Hormuz LNG flows, lowest NW European gas storage in 14 years, and a colder winter forecast.
Second-round effects and wage growth, to be clearer after December.
Rates regime instability: if one of the equity or energy drivers flips, rates can re-price significantly.
vol_and_positioning: 1m realised vol on 10y EUR swaps is 57bp annualised, while implied vol continues to trade at a premium.
Nasdaq 100 is nearly 9% off its early October high; US HY CDX is 20bp wider; OAT/Bund is about 60bp wider.
TTF positioning: less asymmetry to longs at about 98 on Mar27 than a month ago at 72, but convex upside remains in the severe scenario (low supply and cold winter, about 150).
UK front end carries premium (BoE December hike 40% priced) that a clear quarterly signal could remove.
geopolitical: Headlines around a post-midterm re-escalation in the Middle East have raised the risk premium in European natgas.
Hormuz LNG exports are back to 20-25% of pre-war levels and volatile, versus the 65% by January needed in GIR's base case.
UK government deferred defence spending (3% of GDP by 2030) and other spending decisions to next year's Spending Review.

tension_points.bull_case: De-escalation in the Middle East alongside continued equity cracks would drive a sustained rally in rates.
tension_points.bear_case: Equities rebounding on AI resilience while energy stays elevated would drive the next leg higher in yields.
tension_points.what_invalidates: One of the two drivers flipping so that equities and energy line up again, which would warrant a large move in either direction.

tension_points.bull_case: The payoff is still convex in the severe scenario of low supply and a cold winter, with TTF at about 150.
tension_points.bear_case: Mar27 at about 98 already prices a high probability of the low-supply winter, so there is less asymmetry than a month ago when TTF sat at 72.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Hormuz supply recovering, which puts the base case at 70.
